data.text:
Our burger restaurant offers a few main types of burgers for customers to choose from. You can get a classic Beef Burger, a tasty Chicken Burger, or a flavorful Veggie Burger. Once you pick your burger base, you can add various toppings. For example, we have cheese, crispy bacon, fresh lettuce, and ripe tomatoes. You can also add pickles or onions if you like. Sauces like ketchup, mustard, and mayonnaise are always available too.

A customer might order a Beef Burger with just cheese and ketchup. Another person could choose a Chicken Burger with lettuce, tomato, and mayo. Or you could get a Veggie Burger loaded with cheese, pickles, and mustard.

            "Chicken Burger"

                    Bacon

data.text:
I need a route planner that can help me get from one location to another. It should offer different ways to calculate the path, like finding the absolute fastest route or the one that covers the least distance. Sometimes I might even want a route that avoids major highways, perhaps to enjoy the scenic route instead.

The system also needs to consider what kind of vehicle I'm driving. For example, if I have an electric car, it should suggest routes with charging stations along the way. A petrol car, however, might prioritize routes that are most fuel-efficient overall, or even suggest specific refueling stops.
data.code:
include
    Boolean.group-cardinality

features
    RoutePlanner {abstract}
        mandatory
            PathCalculationMethods {abstract}
                alternative
                    FastestRoute
                    ShortestDistanceRoute
                    ScenicRoute
            VehicleTypeConsideration {abstract}
                alternative
                    ElectricCar
                        optional
                            ChargingStationsGuidance
                    PetrolCar
                        optional
                            FuelEfficiencyOptimization
                            RefuelingStopSuggestions

constraints
    ElectricCar => ChargingStationsGuidance

data.text:
A customer approaching the build-your-own salad bar must first select a base for their salad. They are required to choose exactly one type of greens, such as romaine lettuce, spinach, or a spring mix. For example, a customer might choose only spinach as their base.

After choosing the base, the customer can decide on proteins to add. Adding proteins is completely optional; they can choose zero, one, or multiple different protein items. Available options include grilled chicken, tofu, or hard-boiled egg slices. Someone might select both chicken and tofu for their salad.

Next, customers can pick from a wide array of toppings. Like proteins, toppings are optional, allowing for any number of choices from none to several different kinds. Common toppings are tomatoes, cucumbers, shredded carrots, cheese, and croutons. A customer could choose just tomatoes and cheese, or decide they want no extra toppings at all.

Finally, every salad needs a dressing, or the explicit choice to have none. The customer must select one dressing from the available options. These typically include ranch, Caesar, balsamic vinaigrette, or Italian dressing. A customer might pick balsamic vinaigrette, or simply request no dressing on their salad.

When you order a taco, you first pick what kind of tortilla you want. We offer soft corn, soft flour, or a hard crunchy shell. You only get one tortilla type per taco.

Next, you choose your main filling. We have seasoned ground beef, grilled chicken, or slow-cooked pork carnitas. For a vegetarian option, black beans are available. Every taco needs to have one of these fillings.

data.text:
When you set up a new laptop, you get to choose many different parts. You first decide on the central processing unit. For example, you might select an Intel Core i7 for powerful performance, or perhaps an AMD Ryzen 5 for good value.

Then you consider the amount of RAM you need. Most laptops offer options like 8GB, 16GB, or 32GB. Many users find 16GB of RAM to be a solid choice for smooth multitasking.

Storage is another important component. You can often pick between different SSD sizes like 512GB, 1TB, or 2TB. Someone might choose a large 1TB NVMe SSD for fast access to all their files.

The screen resolution also comes with options. Common choices include Full HD, QHD, or 4K displays. A designer might prefer a crisp 4K screen for detailed work.

Lastly, you can usually pick the laptop's color. Standard options are often silver, space gray, or black. Some models might even offer more vibrant colors like a deep blue or a rose gold finish.

    Laptop
        mandatory
            CPU
                alternative
                    "Intel Core i7" {performance 'powerful'}
                    "AMD Ryzen 5" {value 'good'}
            RAM
                alternative
                    "8GB RAM"
                    "16GB RAM" {choice 'solid'}
                    "32GB RAM"

                alternative

data.text:
Imagine a smart home that understands your daily routines. This system connects various devices like lights, a thermostat, security sensors, and a voice assistant. You can control everything easily, often just by speaking or using an app. The goal is to make your home more comfortable, safe, and efficient.

The smart lights aren't just on or off; they can dim or even change color. You could tell your voice assistant, "Set the living room lights to a warm glow." Or, if you leave the house in a hurry, you can turn all lights off remotely from your phone.

Your smart thermostat manages the home's temperature. It can adjust itself based on whether anyone is home or not. For example, it might lower the heat while everyone is at work to save energy. It will then raise it just before you arrive back home.

Security sensors add a layer of safety. These sensors detect things like a door opening or motion in a specific room. If you're away and a window opens, the system can immediately notify your phone.

The voice assistant ties much of it together. You simply speak commands to it to control devices or get information. For example, you could say, "Turn off the kitchen lights and tell me the weather." It makes interacting with your smart home very natural.
data.code:
include
    Boolean
    Type

features
    SmartHome {abstract}
        optional
            Lights {brightness 50, color 'white'}
                optional
                    Dimming
                optional
                    ColorChanging
            Thermostat {set_temperature 22}
                optional
                    PresenceBasedAdjustment
            Security
                optional
                    Sensors {abstract}
                        optional
                            DoorSensor
                        optional
                            MotionSensor
                        optional
                            WindowSensor
                optional
                    Notifications {method 'phone'}
            VoiceAssistant

constraints
    Dimming => VoiceAssistant
    ColorChanging => VoiceAssistant
    WindowSensor => Notifications
    DoorSensor => Notifications
    MotionSensor => Notifications

data.text:
When someone wants to buy a new television, there are several key characteristics they can choose from, which vary widely. These options influence both the performance and the price of the TV.

One major decision is the TV's size. This typically refers to the diagonal measurement of the screen. You can find small TVs around 32 inches, often perfect for a kitchen or small bedroom. Larger options commonly include 55-inch or 65-inch screens for living rooms, with very large models going up to 75 inches or more.

Another important characteristic is the resolution, which dictates how sharp the picture will be. Many standard TVs offer Full HD (1080p), providing a clear image. Most modern TVs now come with 4K Ultra HD, delivering significantly more detail. For the highest clarity, some premium sets are even available with 8K resolution.

The display technology greatly affects picture quality and viewing experience. Standard LED TVs are common and offer good value. OLED technology is known for its perfect blacks and rich colors, as each pixel lights up independently. QLED, another popular technology, enhances brightness and color saturation using quantum dots.

Lastly, smart features are almost standard on new TVs. These capabilities allow the TV to connect to your home internet. This means you can access streaming services like Netflix or Disney+ directly on the TV without needing extra devices. Many smart TVs also include voice control or can integrate with smart home systems.
data.code:
features
    Television
        mandatory
            Size
                alternative
                    "32_inch"
                    "55_inch"
                    "65_inch"
                    "75_inch_or_more"
            Resolution
                alternative
                    "Full_HD_1080p"
                    "4K_Ultra_HD"
                    "8K_Resolution"
            Display_Technology
                alternative
                    Standard_LED
                    OLED
                    QLED
        optional
            Smart_Features

data.text:
This ride-sharing app helps people get around by connecting them with drivers. Users can pick different types of rides based on what they need.

For an economy ride, it's about getting from A to B as cheaply as possible. You'll get a standard car, and it's good for everyday trips. It's the most budget-friendly option available.

If you want a premium ride, you'll get a nicer car and usually a more experienced driver. This is good for special occasions or when you want more comfort. Expect a cleaner, more spacious vehicle.

A shared ride lets multiple passengers go in the same general direction. You might pick up or drop off other people along the way. This helps split the cost, making it cheaper for everyone involved.

You can also schedule a pickup for a specific time in the future. This is helpful if you have an early flight or an important appointment. Just set your pickup time and location in advance, and a driver will be there.
data.code:
features
    "Ride-Sharing App" {abstract}
        alternative
            "Economy Ride"
            "Premium Ride"
            "Shared Ride"
        optional
            "Schedule Pickup"

data.text: You can rent an electric scooter through our system. The way you pay for your ride can vary. You might choose to pay a small fee for every minute you use the scooter. Another option is buying an hourly pass if you plan to ride for a longer time. All scooters are available for pickup and must be returned within defined location zones. If you leave a scooter outside these zones, you could face extra charges.

features
    ScooterRental
        mandatory
            PaymentOptions
                alternative
                    PayPerMinute {minuteRate 0.25}
                    HourlyPass {passPrice 5.0}
            Logistics
                mandatory
                    PickupLocations
                    ReturnHandling
                        alternative
                            ReturnWithinDesignatedZones
                            ReturnOutsideDesignatedZones
        optional

constraints

Another option could be for a family of four, which often uses a convertible dinette and maybe a pop-top bed. Larger vans can even accommodate six people, using bunk beds or an over-cab sleeping area.

The kitchen amenities also vary a lot. A basic kitchen might just have a small sink and a single portable burner. A more common setup includes a two-burner stove and a small refrigerator. Some larger vans even feature a full kitchen with an oven and more counter space.

Lastly, the bathroom type is important. Some vans have no built-in bathroom, relying on external facilities or a portable toilet. A common choice is a wet bath, where the toilet and shower share the same waterproof enclosure. For more comfort, a dry bath offers a completely separate shower stall from the toilet.

data.text:
When a customer books an airline ticket, they first choose their desired service class. For example, they can select an economy class ticket for a standard travel experience. Alternatively, they might opt for a business class ticket, which provides more premium services and comfort. This class selection directly influences the ticket's price and the amenities offered during the flight.

Next, the customer will need to select their specific seat on the aircraft. After confirming their flight and class, they can view a visual seat map. They might choose an aisle seat for easy access or a window seat for views. Certain seats, such as those with extra legroom or in specific zones, might be available for an additional fee.

Finally, the baggage allowance is determined based on their choices. This allowance varies significantly between the chosen class and the specific fare. For instance, an economy ticket might include one carry-on bag and one checked bag up to 23kg. A business class ticket usually permits two checked bags, each up to 32kg, in addition to carry-on items. Overweight or extra bags will typically incur additional charges, which the system must calculate.
data.code:
include
    Boolean.group-cardinality
    Type

features
    AirlineTicketBooking
        mandatory
            ServiceClassSelection
                alternative
                    EconomyClass {price 'Standard', amenities 'Basic'}
                    BusinessClass {price 'Premium', amenities 'Enhanced'}
        optional
            SeatSelection
                alternative
                    AisleSeat
                    WindowSeat
                optional
                    ExtraLegroom {additionalFee true}
                optional
                    SpecificZoneSeat {additionalFee true}
        optional
            CarryOnBag
        optional
            CheckedBag23kg
        optional
            CheckedBag32kg_First
        optional
            CheckedBag32kg_Second

constraints
    EconomyClass => CarryOnBag & CheckedBag23kg
    BusinessClass => CarryOnBag & CheckedBag32kg_First & CheckedBag32kg_Second

data.text:
Banks offer various account types to suit different customer needs. All accounts allow customers to deposit and withdraw money, but they differ in their specific rules and benefits. For instance, a checking account is primarily for everyday transactions and bill payments. It typically has easy access to funds but usually earns very little or no interest. A savings account is designed for growing your money, so it earns interest but might have limits on how often you can withdraw.

Other accounts are more specialized. A student account often waives monthly fees and has lower minimum balance requirements, specifically catering to students. A high-yield account is a type of savings account that offers significantly better interest rates. However, it usually requires a higher minimum balance to qualify for these rates. Some features, like overdraft protection, might be optional additions to certain account types.

When looking at mortgage options, there are a few main things to consider. You can choose between a fixed-rate or a variable-rate mortgage. A fixed-rate means your interest rate stays the same for a specific period, making your monthly payments predictable. For instance, if you get a fixed rate for five years, your payment won't change during that time. A variable-rate mortgage, on the other hand, means your interest rate can go up or down based on market changes.

Then there's the term length, which is how long your current interest rate agreement lasts. Common terms include 1 year, 3 years, or 5 years. A shorter term might have a slightly lower initial rate but you'll renegotiate more often. A longer term provides more stability for your payment over time.

Lastly, you decide on the amortization period. This is the total time you have to pay off the entire mortgage. You might choose an amortization of 20 years, 25 years, or 30 years. A longer amortization means smaller monthly payments, but you end up paying more interest over the full loan duration. A shorter amortization means higher monthly payments but less total interest paid in the long run.

An investment portfolio manages an investor's assets based on their desired level of risk. An investor's risk tolerance can be classified as low, medium, or high. This risk level determines the allocation of different asset types, specifically stocks, bonds, and Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs). For instance, a low-risk portfolio might predominantly feature bonds and stable income-generating ETFs. A medium-risk portfolio could aim for a balanced mix, including a significant portion of stocks, bonds, and diversified ETFs. A high-risk portfolio would likely focus heavily on growth stocks and potentially aggressive ETFs for higher potential returns.

    Boolean.group-cardinality
    Type

        mandatory
            RiskTolerance {abstract}
                alternative
                    LowRisk
                    MediumRisk
                    HighRisk
        optional

        optional
            Bonds
        optional
            ETFs

constraints

    LowRisk => ETFs
    MediumRisk => Stocks
    MediumRisk => Bonds
    MediumRisk => ETFs
    HighRisk => Stocks
    HighRisk => ETFs

When you rent a car, you often get offered different types of insurance. One common type is called Collision Damage Waiver, or CDW. This covers damage to the rental car itself, like if you get into an accident or scratch the door. For example, if a tree branch falls on the rental car and dents the hood, CDW would help pay for the repair.

Then there's liability insurance. This is for damage or injuries you might cause to *other people or their property* while driving the rental car. It doesn't cover your own injuries or the rental car. So, if you accidentally back into another car in a parking lot, liability insurance would cover the damage to *their* car.

Lastly, some policies offer personal effects coverage. This protects your personal belongings that are inside the rental car. If your suitcase or camera gets stolen from the car's trunk, this insurance could help replace them. It's good to consider if you're carrying valuable items.

First, the **fabric** choice is important. For a shirt, this could be 100% cotton, a cotton-polyester blend, or pure linen. The fabric might also come in various colors like blue, red, or green, and could be plain or striped.

Next, the **pattern** defines the garment's look and cut. A pair of pants could be straight-leg, skinny-fit, or bootcut. A dress might have a V-neck or a round neck, and short or long sleeves.

**Sizing** is another key variability. Products are offered in standard sizes such as Small, Medium, Large, and Extra Large. Some items, like trousers, might use numerical waist sizes like 30, 32, 34, along with different inseam lengths.

Finally, the **label type** needs specification. This includes the main brand label, which could be a woven tag or a printed tag inside the garment. There are also care instruction labels, usually small fabric tags sewn into a seam.

data.text: We need a way to describe how we design our product packaging. For example, the box material often changes. Sometimes we use standard corrugated cardboard, other times it's a stronger double-walled kraft board, or a smooth rigid paperboard for luxury items. Inside the box, we might use different inserts. This could be a custom foam piece, a molded plastic tray, or just some shredded paper for padding. The printing on the box can also vary a lot. We might just have a simple one-color logo, or a full-color design with a glossy finish, or even a simple label. Finally, the box dimensions are always changing. A small item might need a 10x10x5 cm box, while a larger product could require something like 50x30x20 cm, or completely custom sizing.
data.code:
features
    "Packaging"
        mandatory
            "Box Material"
                alternative
                    "Corrugated Cardboard"
                    "Double-Walled Kraft Board"
                    "Rigid Paperboard"
            "Printing"
                alternative
                    "One-Color Logo"
                    "Full-Color Glossy Design"
                    "Simple Label"
            "Box Dimensions"
                alternative
                    "Small (10x10x5 cm)"
                    "Large (50x30x20 cm)"
                    "Custom Sizing"
        optional
            "Inserts"
                alternative
                    "Custom Foam Piece"
                    "Molded Plastic Tray"
                    "Shredded Paper"

data.text:
Our software build pipeline automates the process of taking code changes and making them ready for users.

When new code is pushed to a branch, like 'main', the pipeline automatically starts. It first goes through several test stages. This involves running unit tests to check small parts of the code. Then, integration tests verify how different components work together. A quick linting stage also checks code style.

If all tests pass, the pipeline proceeds to deployment. Changes are first deployed to a 'development' environment for internal review. After approval, they move to a 'staging' environment for final checks. Finally, stable versions are deployed to the 'production' environment for our users.

Besides code pushes, opening a pull request also triggers the pipeline to run tests. Occasionally, a full build and test cycle is also scheduled to run overnight. Manual intervention can also start a build if needed.
data.code:
features
    BuildPipeline
        mandatory
            Triggers
                or
                    CodePushTrigger
                    PullRequestTrigger
                    ScheduledBuild
                    ManualTrigger
        mandatory
            PipelineStages
                mandatory
                    TestStages
                        mandatory
                            UnitTests
                            IntegrationTests
                            Linting
                optional
                    DeploymentStages
                        mandatory
                            DeployToDev
                            DeployToStaging
                            DeployToProd

constraints
    DeploymentStages => TestStages
    DeployToProd => DeployToStaging
    DeployToStaging => DeployToDev

data.text: When printing a book, customers need to make several decisions about how their final product will look and feel. One important choice is the paper type for the internal pages. For instance, a novel might use standard cream-colored paper, while a photography book might opt for heavy, bright white stock. Another decision concerns the book's cover. You can choose between a durable hard cover, often seen on textbooks, or a more flexible soft cover, common for many paperbacks. Finally, the cover itself needs a finish. This could be a shiny, glossy finish that makes colors pop, or a sophisticated, non-reflective matte finish for a more subdued look.
data.code:
features
    BookPrinting
        mandatory
            PaperType
                alternative
                    CreamPaper
                    BrightWhitePaper
        mandatory
            Cover
                alternative
                    HardCover
                    SoftCover
                mandatory
                    CoverFinish
                        alternative
                            GlossyFinish
                            MatteFinish

data.text:
Designing a custom home means you get to decide on many features. For example, you can specify the floor plan. This could be an open-concept layout connecting the kitchen and living room, or a more traditional design with distinct, separate rooms. You might want all bedrooms on the second floor, or a master suite downstairs.

Another choice is the number of bedrooms. A couple might only need two bedrooms, one for themselves and one for an office. A larger family might require four or five bedrooms to accommodate everyone comfortably.

Lastly, you select the facade style, which is how the outside of the house looks. You could choose a modern style with lots of glass and flat roofs. Alternatively, a more classic Victorian look with intricate details, or a rustic farmhouse style with a big front porch, are also options.
data.code:
features
    CustomHome {abstract}
        mandatory
            FloorPlan {abstract}
                alternative
                    OpenConcept
                    TraditionalDesign
            BedroomPlacement {abstract}
                alternative
                    AllBedroomsSecondFloor
                    MasterSuiteDownstairs
            NumberOfBedrooms {abstract}
                alternative
                    TwoBedrooms
                    FourBedrooms
                    FiveBedrooms
            FacadeStyle {abstract}
                alternative
                    ModernStyle
                    VictorianLook
                    RusticFarmhouse

data.text: A landscape design system helps plan outdoor spaces by considering many options. For plants, we can choose between various types like shade trees, drought-tolerant shrubs, or colorful flowers, depending on the desired look and climate. Hardscaping involves selecting materials for patios, such as natural stone or concrete, and deciding on features like a winding garden path or a small retaining wall. Irrigation options range from simple manual watering to a fully automated drip system for specific plant zones or a sprinkler system for larger lawns. Lighting decisions include the placement of security lights, accent lights for architectural features, or path lights for safety, often with choices for LED or solar power.

data.text: Selecting paint involves several key decisions. First, a customer must choose whether the paint is for interior or exterior application. This choice often dictates other available features. Next, they select a color, perhaps a vibrant red or a calm grey. The finish is another important factor, with common options like a flat matte, an easy-to-clean satin, or a durable semi-gloss. data.text:
An HVAC system helps control the temperature in a building. It can be set up in different ways.

For example, a house might have a single zone, meaning the whole house has one temperature setting. Another house might have multiple zones, like a living room zone and a bedroom zone, each with its own temperature control.

The type of thermostat also varies. Some homes use a simple manual thermostat where you just set the desired temperature. Others use a programmable thermostat that lets you set a schedule for different temperatures throughout the day. A modern home might have a smart thermostat, which can be controlled remotely and even learn your preferences.

The heating and cooling source also changes. Some systems use a furnace to provide heat, often powered by natural gas or electricity. Other systems use a heat pump, which can both heat and cool the home efficiently. In some cases, a home might even use a hybrid system that combines a furnace with a heat pump.
data.code:
features
    HVAC_System
        mandatory
            Zoning
                alternative
                    Single_Zone
                    Multiple_Zones
        mandatory
            Thermostat_Type
                alternative
                    Manual_Thermostat
                    Programmable_Thermostat
                    Smart_Thermostat
        mandatory
            Heating_Cooling_Source
                alternative
                    Furnace
                    Heat_Pump
                    Hybrid_System

data.text:
A music streaming playlist is a collection of songs organized by a user. Every playlist has an owner who creates it.

A core variability is the playlist's visibility: it can be either public or private. A public playlist means anyone can view its contents, while a private playlist is only accessible to its owner.

Another important choice is whether the playlist is collaborative. A collaborative playlist allows specific invited users to add or remove songs, beyond just the owner. In contrast, a non-collaborative playlist can only be modified by its owner.

Finally, the playback order of songs in a playlist is a key variability. Songs can follow a fixed, pre-defined sequence set by the creator. Alternatively, they can play in a completely random (shuffled) order. Some advanced playlists might even feature a "smart" order, dynamically arranged based on factors like listener preferences or song attributes.
data.code:
features
    Playlist
        alternative
            Public
            Private
        alternative
            Collaborative
            NonCollaborative
        alternative
            FixedOrder
            RandomOrder
            SmartOrder

data.text: This system collects news articles for users. Users can pick specific topics they are interested in, like technology or local events. For example, someone might only want to see articles about science and finance. It also allows users to block certain news sources they don't trust or want to avoid. If a user dislikes articles from "The Daily Scoop," they can block it entirely. Finally, users can set how often they receive news updates. Some might prefer a daily email, while others only want a weekly summary.
data.code:
features
    NewsCollector
        optional
            Topics
                or
                    Technology
                    LocalEvents
                    Science
                    Finance
            BlockedSources
                optional
                    "The Daily Scoop"
            UpdateFrequency
                alternative
                    Daily
                    Weekly

data.text: When you're using digital art software, you have a lot of choices. For brushes, you can pick a soft edge or a hard one, change its size, or make it more transparent. You might also want to select a specific brush shape like a circle or a star. Canvas dimensions are another thing you can customize, setting it to a tiny square or a huge rectangle. You can also decide if your canvas needs a high resolution for printing or a lower one for web use. Lastly, the software lets you choose a color profile, like sRGB for general screens or CMYK if you're preparing for print.
data.code:
features
    Digital_Art_Software {abstract}
        or
            Brushes_Category {default_size 25, max_size 200, default_transparency 0.7}
                alternative
                    Soft_Edge
                    Hard_Edge
                alternative
                    Circle_Shape
                    Star_Shape
            Canvas_Category
                alternative
                    Tiny_Square
                    Huge_Rectangle
                alternative
                    High_Resolution_Print
                    Low_Resolution_Web
            Color_Profile_Category
                alternative
                    sRGB_Profile
                    CMYK_Profile

constraints
    High_Resolution_Print => CMYK_Profile
    Low_Resolution_Web => sRGB_Profile

data.text: This is for a podcast app. Users listen to audio episodes. A key feature is changing playback speed; people like to listen at 1x, 1.5x, or even 2x. They might also want to slow it down sometimes. Another part is how new episodes are managed, some prefer auto-downloading new episodes for all their shows, maybe only on Wi-Fi. Others like to pick and choose what to download manually. There's also a listening queue. Users add episodes to it, and some might want the app to automatically add the next episode from a series they follow.
data.code:
features
    PodcastApp {abstract}
        mandatory
            PlaybackSpeed
                alternative
                    Speed1x
                    Speed1_5x
                    Speed2x
                    CustomSlowSpeed
            EpisodeManagement
                alternative
                    AutoDownloadEpisodes
                        optional
                            OnlyOnWiFi
                    ManualDownload
            ListeningQueue
                optional
                    AutoAddNextEpisode
